quote: Suche z. B die ganze transcendente Gl. für $\lambda$, damit $(\varphi(s))^2 + \lambda \int_a^b\int_a^b K(s;\sigma)\,\varphi(\sigma)\,\varphi(\sigma')\,d\sigma\, d\sigma' = 0$ lösbar ist.
english: Seek, e.g., the entire transcendental equation for lambda such that (phi(s))^2 + lambda ∫∫ K(s;sigma) phi(sigma) phi(sigma') dsigma dsigma' = 0 is solvable.
topic: Notes on a Jacobi-type minimum criterion via regular fields of integrals, a plan to treat nonlinear (quadratic homogeneous) integral equations, and the stability of motion compared with the stability of equilibrium in hydrodynamics.

triage.modern_statement: Take a kernel K(s;σ,σ') on [a,b]^3. (The note writes K(s;σ) but integrates over both σ and σ', so the kernel must depend on σ' too.) The equation is the quadratic, degree-2 homogeneous integral equation φ(s)^2 + λ ∫_a^b∫_a^b K(s;σ,σ') φ(σ) φ(σ') dσ dσ' = 0. Both terms have degree 2 in φ, so if φ is a solution, so is cφ. That makes this a nonlinear eigenvalue problem: find the values of λ for which a nonzero solution φ exists. Hilbert asks whether these 'eigenvalues' are exactly the zeros of a single entire transcendental function of λ, a nonlinear counterpart of the Fredholm determinant D(λ), whose zeros are the eigenvalues of the linear equation φ = λ∫Kφ.
triage.answered_by: No one I could identify. Nonlinear integral equations were developed soon afterwards: E. Schmidt, 'Zur Theorie der linearen und nichtlinearen Integralgleichungen III' (Math. Ann. 65, 1908), on solving nonlinear integral equations and how their solutions branch; then Lyapunov, Lichtenstein, Hammerstein (Acta Math. 54, 1930) and later Krasnosel'skii's topological and positive-operator methods. None of the sources I found builds a Fredholm-type entire function whose zeros are the eigenvalues of a quadratic homogeneous integral equation.

evidence.claim: Schmidt's 1908 Part III treats solving nonlinear integral equations and the branching of their solutions. This is the first systematic follow-up from Hilbert's Göttingen circle, but it uses a Lyapunov–Schmidt-type reduction, not an entire determinant function.
Hammerstein's 'Nichtlineare Integralgleichungen nebst Anwendungen' (Acta Math. 54, 1930, pp. 117–176) became a standard reference for existence theory of nonlinear integral equations.
Later work on Hammerstein-type equations (e.g. Dolph 1949) looks at existence of solutions, not at a characteristic entire function.
A historical survey of nonlinear integral equations names Lyapunov, Poincaré, Hilbert, E. Schmidt, Lalescu, Lichtenstein, Nekrasov, Urysohn and Hammerstein as the early contributors.
Later approaches to nonlinear integral equations, including homogeneous operators and positive solutions, use topological and cone methods (Krasnosel'skii) rather than determinant formulas.

triage.why: The note is a real research question: it asks for an entire-function (Fredholm-determinant) characterization of the eigenvalues of a quadratic homogeneous integral equation. It is not among Hilbert's 23 problems or the 24th problem. The field Hilbert was pointing to did develop, through Schmidt (1908), Hammerstein (1930) and Krasnosel'skii, and nonlinear eigenvalue and spectral theory is still an active area. But those methods (branching theory, variational, topological and cone methods) do not produce a single entire transcendental equation for λ, and none of my sources says whether such a function exists for this equation. My search was cut short by the tool's usage limit, so I could not check more specialized literature (e.g. Lalescu or Lichtenstein on this exact type of equation). I therefore cannot say it was solved, and the 'possibly unexplored' verdict is tentative.
